scenarios.scenario: Engineers keep pasting stack traces and issue details from our SaaS error-tracking service into the conversation by hand. We want Claude to query that service's live data directly, with each engineer signing in through the vendor's browser-based login instead of sharing a long-lived API key.

key.primary: Remote HTTP MCP server (claude mcp add --transport http) with OAuth 2.0 sign-in completed via /mcp or claude mcp login
key.rejected_alternative: A helper shell script or bundled executable that calls the vendor's REST API with a stored personal API key through the Bash tool
key.rejection_reason: The docs designate MCP as the integration path for external tools and data sources, with built-in OAuth 2.0: Claude Code runs the browser flow, stores tokens securely, refreshes them automatically, retries once after a refresh, and flags the server in /mcp when re-authentication is needed. A curl wrapper requires plaintext credential handling and provides none of that, and it exposes no typed tools, resources, or prompts.
key.lifecycle: server connects at session start; the model invokes its tools on demand (discovered via tool search by default); OAuth flow runs when the user authenticates via /mcp or claude mcp login
key.failure_mode: large tool outputs eat context (25,000-token default cap, warning at 10,000), and in non-interactive runs an unauthenticated server's tools stay unavailable until someone completes the OAuth flow in an interactive session

sheets.primary: An MCP server: the vendor's remote HTTP MCP server added with `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` at user scope, with no credential passed on the command line, so each engineer completes the vendor's OAuth 2.0 browser flow themselves via `/mcp` (or `claude mcp login <name>`). The docs use exactly this shape for Sentry: it authenticates through OAuth rather than an API key, so you don't pass a credential when you add it. If the vendor ships an official plugin (for example `sentry` in the official marketplace), install that instead, since it is the same MCP server pre-configured.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill wrapping the vendor's REST API through Bash and curl. It would need a long-lived API key on disk or in an env var, which is precisely the credential model being rejected, and it gives no per-engineer identity or token refresh.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code owns the transport, the OAuth handshake, the stored token, and the refresh-and-retry on 401; it also owns which tools are exposed to the model. The model only decides to call the resulting tools.
sheets.context_boundary: The MCP tool definitions and every tool result land in the main session context window and are billed there each turn. The OAuth handshake happens out of context in the engineer's browser, and the access token is held by Claude Code, so no credential ever enters the transcript.
sheets.lifecycle: The server connects when the session starts and reconnects automatically; the OAuth flow is triggered on first use or whenever the server answers 401 Unauthorized or 403 Forbidden, and can be run ahead of time with `claude mcp login`. An already-signed-in server that returns 401 gets its stored token refreshed and the request retried once. It stops applying when the server is removed, disabled, or the stored authorization is revoked.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed: an unauthenticated or unreachable server is flagged in `/mcp` and its tools simply are not offered, so engineers fall back to pasting stack traces by hand, which is the original problem returning silently. Two specific traps: if a static `headers.Authorization` is configured and the server rejects it, Claude Code reports the connection as failed instead of falling back to OAuth; and some Anthropic-hosted connectors cannot do local OAuth from Claude Code because the upstream identity provider only accepts the redirect URL claude.ai registered.
sheets.version_caveat: OAuth authentication works with HTTP servers only, not the `ws` transport, which is header-only. `claude mcp login <name>` requires Claude Code v2.1.186 or later. Before v2.1.206, a token refresh that failed for a transient reason such as a network error flagged the server as needing authentication for the rest of the session even though the refresh token was still valid. `--callback-port` is available when the vendor requires a pre-registered redirect URI.

sheets.primary: An MCP server connected over remote HTTP/SSE transport using the vendor's own OAuth browser sign-in, registered per engineer (claude mcp add with an http transport, then authorizing via /mcp). Each engineer completes the browser flow and Claude Code stores that user's token locally, so no long-lived shared API key exists.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill documenting curl calls against the vendor's REST API with a shared API key pulled from an environment variable.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness. Claude Code's MCP client owns the transport, the OAuth handshake, token storage and refresh, and which tools are exposed; the model only sees tool schemas and results.
sheets.context_boundary: The server runs out of process or remotely, so its data and the credential stay outside the session. What crosses is the tool list, which stays resident in the main context all session, plus each tool result, which can be very large for stack traces.
sheets.lifecycle: The server connects at session start once configured and its tools stay available until it is removed or disconnects. Authorization is a one-time per-user browser flow with silent refresh, re-triggered only when the grant is revoked or lapses past refresh.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed: an unauthenticated or expired session surfaces as an MCP error and the tools simply do not work, so nobody silently gets stale data. The practical costs are permanent context spend on tool schemas and unbounded result payloads from verbose error-tracker JSON.
sheets.version_caveat: Remote MCP servers with OAuth require a reasonably recent Claude Code, and I do not know the exact minimum version or which MCP spec revision it implements. Enterprise managed settings can also disable MCP servers outright.

sheets.primary: A remote MCP server on the HTTP transport, added with `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` and authenticated per engineer through Claude Code's built-in OAuth 2.0 browser flow from `/mcp` (or `claude mcp login <name>`). This is the documented Sentry-style pattern: the server entry can be shared (project `.mcp.json` or a plugin) while each engineer's token is minted and stored locally.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A local stdio MCP server (or a Bash/curl skill) wrapping the vendor's REST API with a shared API key passed via `--env` or a static `Authorization` header. Rejected because it needs exactly the long-lived shared credential the team wants to avoid, and configuring `headers.Authorization` makes Claude Code report a failed connection rather than falling back to OAuth.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the outcome for connection, token storage, refresh and retry: Claude Code performs the OAuth dance, stores tokens in the OS keychain or credentials file, refreshes on 401 and retries once. The model only owns whether it reaches for those tools instead of asking a human to paste a trace.
sheets.context_boundary: The server runs out of process; the session's main context window receives only tool results (stack traces, issue payloads). With tool search on by default the tool schemas are deferred rather than preloaded, and MCP output warns above 10,000 tokens and is capped at 25,000 by default unless `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` is raised.
sheets.lifecycle: Claude Code connects the server at session start and marks it as needing authentication on 401/403; the browser sign-in is a one-time per-machine step whose token then refreshes automatically. It applies until the server is removed, toggled off in `/mcp`, or credentials are cleared with `claude mcp logout` / Clear authentication.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed: an unauthenticated or unreachable server shows as needing auth or failed, its tools are unavailable, and Claude is told which server failed rather than acting as if it were never configured. The practical gaps are non-interactive runs (`claude -p` and Agent SDK have no `/mcp` panel, so the OAuth flow cannot run and someone must sign in from an interactive session first), and prompt-injection exposure because error payloads are untrusted external content.
sheets.version_caveat: OAuth applies to HTTP servers only; SSE is deprecated and WebSocket is header-auth only. `claude mcp login`/`logout` requires v2.1.186+, no-browser URL fallback v2.1.191+, the re-authenticate notice v2.1.195+, and the non-interactive needs-auth reporting to Claude v2.1.196+. Servers without Dynamic Client Registration need `--client-id` and a fixed `--callback-port`.

sheets.primary: An MCP server over the remote HTTP transport, added per engineer (user scope so it follows the person rather than a repo) with `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>`, exactly the shape the docs use for the Sentry error-tracking server. Each engineer completes the vendor's OAuth 2.0 browser sign-in from `/mcp` or `claude mcp login <name>`, so no shared long-lived API key exists anywhere.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that shells out to the vendor's REST API with a shared API key: it gives no per-engineer identity, puts a long-lived secret on every machine, and the docs point at MCP precisely for the copy-data-into-chat-from-a-monitoring-tool case.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: Claude Code holds the connection, stores and automatically refreshes the OAuth token, and runs the per-tool permission prompt. The model only decides when to call a tool; it never sees or handles the credential.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session context window. Tool names load into the session (schemas can be deferred through tool search) and only bounded tool results cross back, capped by MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS; the browser flow and token storage stay outside the conversation entirely.
sheets.lifecycle: The server connects at session start once configured, and the OAuth flow runs once per engineer in the browser; after that the stored token is refreshed automatically, and on a 401 Claude Code refreshes, reconnects and retries the request once. It stops applying on `claude mcp logout <name>`, on Clear authentication in the `/mcp` menu, or when the server entry is removed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. A server that cannot connect or that needs authentication simply contributes no tools and the run continues, so the model cannot distinguish an absent tool from a declining one. In non-interactive `claude -p` runs there is no `/mcp` panel to complete sign-in, and if you configure `headers.Authorization` and the server rejects it, Claude Code reports the connection as failed instead of falling back to OAuth.
sheets.version_caveat: OAuth works on the HTTP transport (SSE is deprecated, WebSocket has no OAuth path). `claude mcp login` requires v2.1.186+; the startup needs-authentication notice requires v2.1.193+; from v2.1.196 a headless run is told the server's tools are unavailable rather than that they do not exist; before v2.1.206 a transient refresh failure flagged the server for the rest of the session.

scenarios.scenario: Claude keeps introducing type errors on our TypeScript codebase that it only discovers when the test suite finally runs. We want it to see compiler diagnostics immediately after each edit and to jump to definitions and references instead of grepping for symbol names.

key.primary: Install the official typescript-lsp plugin from the claude-plugins-official marketplace, with the typescript-language-server binary installed separately on each machine
key.rejected_alternative: Author a custom plugin containing an .lsp.json entry that launches typescript-language-server
key.rejection_reason: The docs explicitly direct users to install the pre-built LSP plugins for common languages (TypeScript, Python, Rust) from the official marketplace and to create custom LSP plugins only for languages not already covered. A hand-rolled config duplicates a maintained plugin, and if both end up enabled, only the first server registered for the .ts extension starts while the other is silently ignored with a /plugin warning.
key.lifecycle: language server starts when the plugin is enabled; diagnostics are pushed into Claude's context after each edit; navigation (go to definition, find references, hover) is available on demand
key.failure_mode: the plugin does not bundle the language server binary: without typescript-language-server on PATH the server fails with Executable not found in $PATH in the /plugin Errors tab and no diagnostics ever appear

sheets.primary: An LSP server delivered as a plugin: install `typescript-lsp` from the official `claude-plugins-official` marketplace, after installing the `typescript-language-server` binary. That plugin is just a `.lsp.json` mapping `.ts`/`.tsx` to the language server, and it turns on both halves of the request: automatic diagnostics pushed into Claude's context after every edit, and code navigation (go to definition, find references, hover, implementations, call hierarchies) instead of grep.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook running `tsc --noEmit` after each Write or Edit. It catches type errors but is a full project typecheck per edit rather than incremental server diagnostics, and it gives no definitions, references, or hover, so it solves only half the need at much higher latency.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code starts and supervises the language server process, and pushes diagnostics into Claude's context after edits on its own (`diagnostics` defaults to true). The model does not choose to run the typechecker.
sheets.context_boundary: The language server runs out of context as a subprocess owned by Claude Code. Only the diagnostic summaries after each edit and the results of explicit navigation requests cross into the main session context; the server's full index and protocol traffic never do. The user sees an indicator such as 'Found 3 new diagnostic issues in 2 files' and presses Ctrl+O to read them.
sheets.lifecycle: The server starts when the plugin is enabled and the session begins, claims the file extensions declared in `extensionToLanguage`, and runs for the session. `/reload-plugins` restarts plugin LSP servers. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled, when the server crashes past `maxRestarts`, or when another enabled server registered the same extension first, in which case this one never starts at all.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open, which is the dangerous shape here: if the binary is missing you get `Executable not found in $PATH` in the `/plugin` Errors tab and Claude quietly goes back to grepping, with no error at the point of use. A configuration that is invalid (missing `command` or `extensionToLanguage`) is skipped entirely, with the reason visible only under `claude --debug`. Other practical failures: large monorepos produce false-positive unresolved-import diagnostics, and servers like pyright and rust-analyzer can consume significant memory.
sheets.version_caveat: `restartOnCrash` and `shutdownTimeout` require Claude Code v2.1.205 or later; before v2.1.205 the schema accepted both but setting either caused Claude Code to skip that LSP server entirely at startup, visible only in `claude --debug`. Also before v2.1.205, a server that failed to initialize still claimed its extensions and blocked another valid server for the same extension. The plugin never installs the language server binary for you.

sheets.primary: An LSP plugin: install `typescript-lsp` from the official marketplace, or ship your own plugin with a `.lsp.json` mapping `.ts`/`.tsx` to `typescript-language-server`. Claude Code then pushes language-server diagnostics into Claude's context immediately after each edit and exposes go-to-definition, find-references, hover, symbols and call hierarchy as navigation instead of grep.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook that runs `tsc --noEmit` after every Write/Edit and feeds the output back. Rejected because it delivers diagnostics only, gives no symbol navigation, and re-typechecks the project on every single edit.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness: Claude Code starts and supervises the language server process, injects diagnostics automatically after edits, and provides navigation as a tool surface. The model owns only whether it acts on a reported error and whether it prefers navigation over grep.
sheets.context_boundary: The language server is a separate long-lived subprocess. What crosses into the main session context window is the diagnostic text after each edit plus any navigation results the model requests, so every edit carries a small recurring token cost.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the plugin is enabled and the workspace has been trusted, runs for the session, restarts on crash up to `maxRestarts`, and stops on session end or plugin disable. Setting `diagnostics: false` keeps navigation while suppressing automatic diagnostic injection.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and silently: if the language server binary is missing, Claude Code records `Executable not found in $PATH` in the `/plugin` Errors tab and Claude just keeps grepping with no visible degradation. Monorepos generate false-positive unresolved-import diagnostics, large projects make the server memory-hungry, and when two enabled servers claim `.ts` only the first registered one starts.
sheets.version_caveat: The plugin does not ship the binary: `npm install -g typescript-language-server typescript` is a prerequisite. `restartOnCrash` and `shutdownTimeout` require v2.1.205 or later, and before v2.1.205 setting either caused Claude Code to skip the server entirely with the reason visible only under `claude --debug`. LSP servers start only after workspace trust.

sheets.primary: An LSP server delivered as a plugin component: the official `typescript-lsp` plugin from the marketplace, or a custom plugin whose `.lsp.json` (or `lspServers` in plugin.json) declares `command: typescript-language-server` with `extensionToLanguage` for .ts/.tsx and `diagnostics: true`. LSP has no standalone authoring path, so shipping this means shipping a plugin.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook running `tsc --noEmit` after every Edit: it is mechanically enforceable but pays a whole-project type check per edit and answers only half the need, since it gives no go-to-definition or find-references.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, and neither half is a guarantee: the harness starts the language server and pushes diagnostics into Claude's context after edits, while the model owns whether it acts on them. Nothing here can block a bad edit.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session window. The language server runs as a separate process outside the context; diagnostics are injected into Claude's context after edits and definition/reference lookups come back as ordinary tool results in the same window.
sheets.lifecycle: Per server: resolve the workspace root and extension map, start the server after workspace trust, publish diagnostics after edits, serve definition/references/hover, restart on crash (`restartOnCrash` defaults to true, bounded by `maxRestarts`), and shut down at plugin disable or session end. A plugin update mid-session keeps the old path until `/reload-plugins`.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and quiet. The binary is not bundled, so a missing `typescript-language-server` shows `Executable not found in $PATH` in the `/plugin` Errors tab and Claude silently degrades to grep-quality answers; an invalid server config is skipped with the reason visible only under `claude --debug`; and when two enabled servers claim `.ts`, the first registered wins and the other never starts.
sheets.version_caveat: `restartOnCrash` and `shutdownTimeout` require Claude Code v2.1.205 or later: before that the schema was accepted but setting either caused Claude Code to skip that LSP server entirely at startup. Also before v2.1.205 a server that failed to initialize still claimed its extensions and blocked another valid server.

sheets.primary: LSP integration: configure a TypeScript language server for Claude Code so the harness runs it, injects compiler diagnostics right after each edit, and provides go-to-definition and find-references instead of grep. Teams already in VS Code or JetBrains get the same diagnostics channel through the official IDE integration.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PostToolUse hook that runs tsc --noEmit after every Edit.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness. The language server is a harness-managed process and diagnostics are injected automatically after edits; the model does not have to remember to ask for them.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session context. The server's project index and memory live in its own process; only the diagnostics for touched files and the definition/reference results cross into the transcript.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the session or workspace opens, or when the first matching file is touched, runs for the session, and stops at session end. It does not apply to files outside the configured language's file patterns.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory once the diagnostics land: the model can still read a type error and press on. It fails open if the server never starts or is still indexing, so the absence of diagnostics looks identical to clean code, and on a large monorepo it is memory hungry and can lag an edit by seconds.
sheets.version_caveat: Native LSP configuration in Claude Code is recent and I am not confident of the exact settings key or the minimum version, so verify the current field name before writing config. IDE-supplied diagnostics instead require the official extension installed and connected.

scenarios.scenario: Our platform team maintains a set of code-review helpers, reusable workflow commands, edit-time automations, and a shared external-tool configuration. Every engineer who clones any of our repositories should be offered the same set automatically and should receive updates whenever we publish changes.

key.primary: Package everything as a plugin, distribute it through a plugin marketplace (marketplace.json in a git repo), and reference it from each repository's .claude/settings.json via extraKnownMarketplaces plus enabledPlugins so teammates are prompted on workspace trust
key.rejected_alternative: Commit the raw .claude/ directories (commands/, agents/, skills/, hooks in settings.json) into every repository
key.rejection_reason: Standalone .claude/ configuration is documented as per-project, unversioned, and manually copied to share. The docs designate plugins plus marketplaces for exactly this need: sharing with teammates, versioned releases, reuse across projects, and automatic update tracking, with extraKnownMarketplaces prompting collaborators to install when they trust the project folder.
key.lifecycle: marketplace registration is offered when a teammate trusts the repo folder; plugins install and enable per enabledPlugins; updates flow via /plugin marketplace update and the plugin's version resolution
key.failure_mode: a version string pinned in plugin.json that nobody bumps means pushed changes never reach installers, and teammates who never accept the workspace trust dialog are never prompted, silently missing the tooling

sheets.primary: A plugin distributed through a team marketplace, wired into each repository by settings rather than by copying files. Put the review helpers in `skills/`, the workflow commands in `skills/` or `commands/`, the edit-time automations in `hooks/hooks.json`, and the external-tool configuration in the plugin's own `.mcp.json`, publish it from a git-hosted marketplace, then add `extraKnownMarketplaces` plus `enabledPlugins` to each repository's `.claude/settings.json`. When team members trust the repository folder, Claude Code prompts them to install these marketplaces and plugins.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Committing a `.claude/` directory with standalone skills, commands and hooks into every repository. It gives no versioning and no update path: each of the many repositories holds its own drifting copy that someone has to re-sync by hand every time the platform team publishes a change.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness for loading and updating (Claude Code reads `extraKnownMarketplaces`/`enabledPlugins`, resolves the marketplace, installs and auto-updates), with a human consent gate: the engineer must trust the workspace folder and accept the install prompt. The model owns nothing here.
sheets.context_boundary: Plugin components load into each engineer's main session context: skills and agents as loadable definitions, MCP tool schemas as tool definitions, with a per-turn token cost the `/plugin` detail view estimates as 'Context cost'. Hooks and MCP servers execute in their own processes outside the context window and only their output crosses back.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered when an engineer opens a repository whose `.claude/settings.json` names the marketplace and trusts the folder; Claude Code then prompts to install. Updates arrive through marketplace auto-update, which runs in the background after session start with a random delay of up to ten minutes, so the running session keeps its loaded versions until `/reload-plugins` or the next launch. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, or when the marketplace is removed, which uninstalls everything installed from it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open at the consent boundary: the set is offered, not imposed. An engineer who declines the trust prompt or the install prompt simply works without the helpers and hooks, silently, so you get inconsistent enforcement across the team rather than a hard failure. Auto-update is disabled by default for third-party marketplaces, so without turning it on people sit on stale versions. To actually mandate the set you need managed settings, which install at managed scope and cannot be modified by users.
sheets.version_caveat: As of Claude Code v2.1.195 the install step applies on every path that loads plugins: a plugin that only the project's `.claude/settings.json` enables, and that comes from an external source such as a GitHub repository or npm package, does not load until the team member installs it, and Claude Code reports it as not installed. The scope-choice dialog when uninstalling a project-enabled plugin requires v2.1.203 or later. Administrators can set `"autoUpdate": true` on each `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry in managed settings.

sheets.primary: One plugin bundling all four component types (skills for the review helpers, workflows for the reusable commands, hooks/hooks.json for the edit-time automations, .mcp.json for the shared external-tool config), published from a git-hosted team marketplace. Each repository checks in `.claude/settings.json` declaring the marketplace under `extraKnownMarketplaces` plus the plugins under `enabledPlugins`, which is the documented way to have teammates prompted automatically.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Copying a standalone `.claude/` directory into every repository: same components, but no versioning, no rollback, no update path, and each repo's copy drifts independently.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns discovery and loading (it reads the settings keys, prompts on workspace trust, and installs from the marketplace), but the offer itself is a prompt the engineer can decline, so adoption is not guaranteed by the mechanism.
sheets.context_boundary: Installation and refresh happen outside the conversation, in the plugin cache. Once enabled, the components load into every session in that repo: skill descriptions in the listing, hooks in the harness process, MCP tool names in the session window.
sheets.lifecycle: Team members are prompted to install the marketplace when they trust the project folder; components load per session while the plugin is enabled; a user's `enabledPlugins` entry at any scope persists across plugin updates and reinstalls; it stops on `/plugin disable` or uninstall. Updates arrive by marketplace refresh, `/plugin update`, or background auto-update.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and advisory at the offer step: a declined prompt leaves that engineer with none of it, and a rejected manifest fails every bundled component together. Background auto-update refreshes disable git credential helpers, so a private HTTPS marketplace falls back to a full re-clone that can time out, leaving teammates silently pinned to the last synced state.
sheets.version_caveat: `enabledPlugins` still honours project and local settings, but since v2.1.207 `pluginConfigs` option values are ignored in project settings (user, --settings and managed only), so a cloned repo cannot supply plugin option values. `defaultEnabled: false` requires v2.1.154+, and `renames` for a later plugin rename requires v2.1.193+.

sheets.primary: A plugin published through a team-owned plugin marketplace (a git repository), bundling the review commands, the reusable slash commands, the edit-time hooks, and the MCP server configuration as one unit. Each repository's checked-in .claude/settings.json names the marketplace and the plugin, so a fresh clone offers the same set automatically.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Copying a .claude directory of commands, hooks and .mcp.json into every repository by hand.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness for installation, loading and hook execution; the user owns the one-time trust decision; the model only consumes the resulting commands and skills.
sheets.context_boundary: Session context, on demand: slash command and skill bodies load when invoked while skill descriptions stay resident, and the hooks plus the MCP server run in harness-owned processes outside the model's window.
sheets.lifecycle: Repo settings advertise the marketplace, so the first session in a clone prompts to install and trust it; updates arrive when the marketplace is refreshed. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled or the engineer works outside those repositories.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on adoption: an engineer who declines or dismisses the prompt silently gets none of the automations and nothing reports the gap, so consistency is assumed rather than proven. It also means executable hook code ships centrally, so a bad merge or a compromised marketplace runs on every machine.
sheets.version_caveat: Plugins and marketplaces were still marked beta in the 2.0 line, and I do not know the exact minimum version or whether the settings keys are still named extraKnownMarketplaces and enabledPlugins. Managed enterprise policy can block plugin installation entirely.

sheets.primary: One plugin holding all four pieces (skills/commands for the review helpers and workflows, `hooks/hooks.json` for the edit-time automations, `.mcp.json` for the shared external-tool configuration), published through a team plugin marketplace, and referenced from each repository's checked-in `.claude/settings.json` using `extraKnownMarketplaces` plus `enabledPlugins`, with marketplace auto-update enabled.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Standalone `.claude/` configuration copied into each repository (commands, agents, and hooks in `settings.json`). Rejected because there is no update channel: every repo drifts independently and changes must be hand-propagated.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns distribution and loading: fetching the marketplace, prompting for install on folder trust, running the hooks, and starting the MCP servers. The model owns only whether it invokes the review skills and workflow commands.
sheets.context_boundary: Skills, agents and MCP tool definitions load into each engineer's main session context and cost tokens every turn, which the `/plugin` detail view surfaces as a Context cost estimate. Hooks and the MCP server run in their own processes; only their output crosses back into the window.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered when a teammate trusts the repository folder: Claude Code prompts to install the declared marketplaces and plugins, components load at session start, and `/reload-plugins` applies mid-session changes. It stops applying when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled, or the repo entry is removed (removing a marketplace uninstalls its plugins).
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open at the install gate, because it is an offer rather than a mandate. A plugin that only the project's `.claude/settings.json` enables and that comes from an external source does not load until the engineer runs the install; Claude Code just reports it as not installed and prints the `claude plugin install` command. Auto-update also fires after startup with up to a ten-minute random delay, so a running session keeps the version it launched with until reload.
sheets.version_caveat: The install-prompt-on-every-plugin-load-path behavior requires v2.1.195 or later. Auto-update is on by default only for official Anthropic marketplaces; third-party and local marketplaces default to off, though admins can set `"autoUpdate": true` on the `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry in managed settings. `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` suppresses updates unless `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1` is also set, and `strictKnownMarketplaces` can restrict which marketplaces are allowed.

scenarios.scenario: We ship an internal deployment CLI, a compiled binary with many subcommands. Whenever our shared toolkit is active, Claude should be able to run it as a bare command inside ordinary shell pipelines, composing it with grep and jq across every project, without anyone editing their PATH.

key.primary: Ship the binary in the plugin's bin/ directory, which is added to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled
key.rejected_alternative: Wrap the CLI in a stdio MCP server that exposes each subcommand as a separate MCP tool
key.rejection_reason: MCP tools have fixed input schemas and their results flow through MCP output limits, so they cannot participate in shell pipelines or compose with other commands. The plugin bin/ directory exists precisely for this: files there are invokable as bare commands in any Bash tool call while the plugin is enabled, keeping normal CLI ergonomics.
key.lifecycle: executables are on the Bash tool's PATH whenever the plugin is enabled; invocation happens through ordinary Bash tool calls under the normal permission flow
key.failure_mode: no structured schema constrains usage, so the model can misuse flags a typed tool would have prevented, and the command vanishes from PATH the moment the plugin is disabled, breaking workflows that assumed it

sheets.primary: Ship the compiled binary in the toolkit plugin's `bin/` directory. Files there are added to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled and are invokable as bare commands in any Bash tool call, so `deployctl status | jq .` composes normally with no PATH edits by users.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An MCP server wrapping the CLI's subcommands: it is the governed way to expose an external system, but its tools are model-invoked calls that cannot be piped into grep or jq inside a shell pipeline, which is the whole requirement here.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: Claude Code injects the plugin's `bin/` into the PATH of the Bash tool while the plugin is enabled. The model owns only the pipeline it writes, and normal Bash permission rules still apply to the resulting command.
sheets.context_boundary: The main session, executing in a Bash tool subprocess. Only the command's stdout/stderr crosses back into the conversation; the binary and the PATH injection live outside it.
sheets.lifecycle: The PATH entry exists for Bash tool calls for as long as the plugin is enabled in a scope that applies to the current project, and disappears on `/plugin disable` or uninstall. Because the plugin's installation directory changes on update, a mid-session update keeps the previous path until the components are reloaded.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open as a plain command-not-found: if the plugin is not enabled in that scope the pipeline just errors, with nothing announcing why. A file that is not executable or lacks a valid shebang will not run (`chmod +x`), and the PATH injection reaches Bash tool calls only, so a compiled binary must match each user's platform.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate, experimental marker, or enabling flag is documented for `bin/`: it appears in the plugin component tables as a standard root directory, unlike monitors and themes which must be declared under `experimental.*`. Loading the plugin from a ZIP archive during testing does require v2.1.128 or later.

sheets.primary: Ship the compiled binary in the plugin's `bin/` directory at the plugin root. Executables placed there are added to the Bash tool's `PATH` while the plugin is enabled, so the CLI is invokable as a bare command inside any Bash tool call and composes normally with grep and jq, in every project, with no user PATH edits.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Wrapping the CLI as a bundled stdio MCP server exposing each subcommand as a tool. Rejected because MCP tools are structured tool invocations, not shell words: they cannot be piped into grep or jq, which is precisely the composition requirement here.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness: Claude Code injects the plugin's `bin/` into the PATH it hands the Bash tool. The model owns constructing correct invocations, and the permission system still gates each Bash call as usual.
sheets.context_boundary: The binary runs in the Bash tool's subprocess, outside the model's context; only stdout and stderr cross back into the session window. The PATH change is scoped to Claude Code's Bash tool, not to the user's interactive shell or other processes.
sheets.lifecycle: Available from the moment the plugin is loaded and enabled (session start, or after `/reload-plugins` if enabled mid-session) and for every Bash call in that session across all projects. It disappears when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly: a missing executable bit, a wrong shebang, or a binary built for another OS or architecture surfaces only as `command not found` from the shell, after which Claude improvises absolute paths. A single compiled binary is platform-specific, so one plugin copy will not serve mac, Linux and Windows teammates without per-platform builds. Bash permission rules also need to allow the command name or every call prompts.
sheets.version_caveat: The docs list `bin/` as a plugin-root directory with no version gate stated beyond a Claude Code version that supports plugins, and there is no `bin` field in the manifest schema, so the directory must literally be `bin/` at the plugin root rather than a configurable path. Because `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` changes on update and the old directory is pruned about two weeks later, anything that hard-codes an absolute path to the binary needs `/reload-plugins` after an update.

sheets.primary: Ship the binary inside the shared plugin and get its directory onto the PATH used for Bash tool calls, via a plugin-declared bin directory if the manifest supports one, otherwise an env/PATH entry contributed by settings at install. Being on PATH is what lets Claude use it as a bare command inside grep and jq pipelines.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An MCP server that wraps each subcommand of the CLI as a separate tool.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness: it builds the environment for every Bash invocation, so whether the command resolves is not a model decision. The model owns only how it composes the pipeline.
sheets.context_boundary: Execution happens in the Bash tool's own process, so only the command line and its stdout/stderr cross into the session context. That is precisely why filtering with grep/jq in the pipe is cheaper than an MCP tool returning full JSON into the window.
sheets.lifecycle: Available to every Bash call in any session where the plugin is enabled, in every project, with no per-project setup and no user PATH edit. It disappears when the plugin is disabled or uninstalled.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly: if the PATH contribution does not apply, the shell reports command not found and the model tends to improvise another route rather than flag the missing tool. Vendoring a compiled binary also breaks across OS and architecture unless per-platform builds ship.
sheets.version_caveat: I am not certain Claude Code plugins have a documented manifest field that prepends a bin directory to PATH, so verify that before relying on it and fall back to a settings env entry. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is the documented way for plugin content to reference its own files.

sheets.primary: A plugin with a `bin/` directory holding the deployment binary (or a thin wrapper that execs it). Files in a plugin's `bin/` are added to the Bash tool's `PATH` and are invokable as bare commands in any Bash tool call while the plugin is enabled, so Claude can write `deploy status | jq '.services[]' | grep degraded` with no absolute path and nobody edits their shell profile.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Wrapping the CLI in an MCP server so each subcommand becomes a tool. That loses exactly what was asked for: MCP tool results come back as tool output, not as a stream you can pipe into `grep` and `jq`, and every subcommand would have to be modelled as a separate tool schema that costs context on every turn.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code injects the plugin's `bin/` onto the `PATH` of the Bash tool's environment while the plugin is enabled. The model just types the bare command name; it is not responsible for locating the binary.
sheets.context_boundary: The binary executes in a Bash subprocess, entirely outside the context window. Only the pipeline's stdout and stderr cross back into the main session context, so a large subcommand dump is a context cost the model must manage with `head`, `jq` filters, or redirection. The binary's own help text and subcommand surface are not preloaded, which is why a skill documenting the subcommands is a useful companion.
sheets.lifecycle: `PATH` injection is active for the whole time the plugin is enabled, from plugin load onward, and applies to every Bash tool call in every project the plugin is enabled for. It stops the moment the plugin is disabled or uninstalled. On a plugin update `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` changes, so anything resolving the binary by absolute path breaks while the bare name keeps working.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed at the shell: if the plugin is disabled, the file lacks the executable bit, or the shipped binary is the wrong OS/architecture for that engineer's machine, the command dies with 'command not found' or an exec error, and the model is prone to improvise a wrong absolute path or a substitute command instead of reporting the real cause. The injection is scoped to the Bash tool, so it does not help hook commands, monitors, or the engineer's own terminal, which is a common source of 'it works for Claude but not for me'.
sheets.version_caveat: The plugin docs document `bin/` only as a default plugin-root folder, with no corresponding manifest key and no stated minimum Claude Code version or experimental gate, so unlike `monitors` and `themes` it is not an experimental component. The practical gate is not a version but packaging: shipping a compiled binary through a marketplace means shipping per-platform builds, since the plugin is copied verbatim into `~/.claude/plugins/cache` and cannot reference files outside its own directory.

scenarios.scenario: The tooling bundle we distribute internally changes daily. Teammates should automatically receive every merged commit as an update, with zero release bookkeeping on our side.

key.primary: Omit the version field from both plugin.json and the marketplace entry so Claude Code falls back to the git commit SHA as the version, treating every commit as a new version
key.rejected_alternative: Maintain a semantic version field in plugin.json and bump it for each release
key.rejection_reason: The version string is the cache key that decides whether an update exists: with an explicit version set, pushing new commits without bumping it has no effect and /plugin update reports already at the latest version. The docs' version-management table recommends commit-SHA versioning for internal or team plugins under active development and warn against explicit versions when iterating quickly.
key.lifecycle: version is resolved when /plugin update or auto-update fires: plugin.json version first, then marketplace entry version, then the git commit SHA, then unknown
key.failure_mode: every commit becomes an update, so teammates churn through half-finished work; and if someone later adds a version field for one release and forgets it, users freeze on that string while commits keep landing

sheets.primary: Keep the bundle as a plugin served from a git-backed marketplace whose entry tracks the repository's default branch rather than tagged releases, so the installed content is whatever that branch currently holds and every merged commit becomes the shipped version.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Cutting semver releases (npm or GitHub releases) and pinning a version in each plugin entry.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness. Fetching and swapping plugin content is a Claude Code operation; the model plays no part and cannot be blamed for a stale install.
sheets.context_boundary: Nothing about the update crosses into the model's context except the resulting commands and skills. Distribution happens in the harness and on disk, generally between sessions.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered by a marketplace or plugin update check rather than continuously, and a session already running keeps whatever it loaded at start. It stops when the plugin is removed or the entry is pinned to a tag.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open with no gate: a broken merge propagates to everyone with no review step and no simple rollback, and two engineers can sit on different commits for a whole day. With no version identifier, reproducing a colleague's bug becomes guesswork.
sheets.version_caveat: I do not know whether current Claude Code refreshes marketplace plugins automatically or only on an explicit update command, and that detail decides whether every merged commit truly lands with zero action from teammates. Plugin marketplaces are still beta.

sheets.primary: A plugin published from a git-hosted marketplace with commit-SHA versioning: omit the `version` field from both `plugin.json` and the marketplace entry, so Claude Code falls back to the git commit SHA of the plugin's source and users get updates on every new commit to the plugin's git source. Pair that with auto-update enabled on the marketplace so the refresh happens without anyone running `/plugin update`. The docs name this exact approach as the one for internal or team plugins under active development.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Explicit semver in `plugin.json`. It is the wrong shape for a daily-changing bundle: users get updates only when you bump the field, so every merge would need a version bump, which is precisely the release bookkeeping being eliminated.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code computes the plugin's version, uses it as the cache key that decides whether an update is available, and runs the background auto-update. Neither the model nor the publisher touches the update path once the source is configured.
sheets.context_boundary: Nothing about versioning enters the session context window. The update runs as background work on the user's machine; the newly loaded components announce themselves in content appended to the conversation only after `/reload-plugins` or at the next launch.
sheets.lifecycle: Auto-update fires after the session starts, with a random delay of up to ten minutes, so the running session keeps using the versions it loaded at launch. If plugins were updated you get a notification prompting `/reload-plugins`, otherwise the new versions load on the next launch. It stops when the plugin is uninstalled, when the marketplace is removed (which uninstalls its plugins), or when `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` is set.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and silently, in one specific way: if anyone sets `version` in `plugin.json` or in the marketplace entry, SHA-based versioning is bypassed and pushing new commits alone stops delivering anything, while `/plugin update` cheerfully reports 'already at the latest version'. The second silent failure is that auto-update is disabled by default for third-party and local development marketplaces, so without toggling it on, teammates keep whatever they installed. Also note that every merged commit reaching everyone means a bad commit reaches everyone too, with no release gate.
sheets.version_caveat: Commit-SHA versioning only applies to `github`, `url`, `git-subdir`, and relative-path sources in a git-hosted marketplace; `npm` sources and local directories not inside a git repository resolve to the version `unknown` instead. Auto-update defaults to on only for official Anthropic marketplaces; administrators can set `"autoUpdate": true` on each `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry in managed settings. `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` turns off all automatic updates, and `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1` keeps plugin updates while disabling Claude Code's own.

sheets.primary: Distribute the bundle as a plugin from a git-hosted marketplace and omit `version` from both `plugin.json` and the marketplace entry. Claude Code then resolves the version from the git commit SHA of the plugin's source and treats every commit as a new version, so a merge is the release. Enable auto-update on the marketplace so it lands without user action.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An explicit semver `version` in `plugin.json` with a CHANGELOG per release. Rejected because with `version` set, pushing commits is not enough: users only receive changes when the field is bumped and `/plugin update` otherwise reports already at the latest version, which is exactly the bookkeeping to be avoided.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness entirely. Version resolution, the cache-key comparison, and the background auto-update pass are Claude Code's; nothing here depends on the model behaving.
sheets.context_boundary: The update machinery runs outside the model's context. Only the resulting components occupy the session window, and after a reload the newly loaded components announce themselves in appended content while the earlier history still reads from the prompt cache.
sheets.lifecycle: Auto-update runs shortly after session startup with a random delay of up to ten minutes; the running session keeps its launched versions, and you are prompted to run `/reload-plugins` or pick them up at next launch. It stops on uninstall, on marketplace removal, or when `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` is set without `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1`.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and unpinned: everyone silently tracks HEAD, so a broken commit propagates to the whole team with no review gate and no version to roll back to. Each superseded version directory lingers in the cache as an orphan for about fourteen days. Auto-update also defaults to off for third-party and local marketplaces, so if nobody enables it the daily commits never reach anyone.
sheets.version_caveat: Commit-SHA fallback applies only to `github`, `url`, `git-subdir`, and relative-path sources inside a git-hosted marketplace; `npm` sources and local directories outside a git repo resolve to `unknown` and never look updated. A `version` in `plugin.json` beats one in the marketplace entry, so both must be left unset. `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1` keeps plugin updates flowing when Claude Code's own updater is disabled.

sheets.primary: Distribute the plugin from a git-hosted marketplace and omit `version` from both plugin.json and the marketplace entry, so Claude Code falls back to the git commit SHA and every merged commit is automatically treated as a new version. Leave the marketplace source unpinned (no `ref` or `sha`) so teammates track the moving branch and background auto-update pulls it.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A pinned semantic `version` in plugin.json bumped per release: that is exactly the release bookkeeping the team wants to avoid, and forgetting one bump strands every user on the cached copy with no error.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it end to end: version resolution, cache-path selection and the git pull are Claude Code's plugin updater. No model judgment is involved.
sheets.context_boundary: Entirely outside the conversation. The clone/pull lands in the local plugin cache under ~/.claude/plugins; only the loaded components afterwards occupy session context.
sheets.lifecycle: Version resolves in order: plugin.json `version`, then the marketplace entry `version`, then the git commit SHA. A new commit means a new resolved version and a new cache path, picked up by background auto-update or `/plugin update`; a mid-session update leaves hooks, MCP and LSP servers on the old path until `/reload-plugins`, and monitors until a session restart.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails silently stale rather than loudly. If anyone sets `version` in plugin.json, pushed commits never reach existing users because the resolved version string is unchanged, and plugin.json silently wins over a marketplace-entry version. Private-marketplace background pulls run without git credential helpers, so HTTPS refreshes fall back to a re-clone that may time out and leave users on the last synced state.
sheets.version_caveat: The commit-SHA fallback only applies to git-based sources (`github`, `url`, `git-subdir`, and relative paths inside a git-hosted marketplace); npm and non-git local sources have no SHA to fall back to. `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_KEEP_MARKETPLACE_ON_FAILURE=1` keeps the existing clone when a background pull fails, and `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_GIT_TIMEOUT_MS` raises the clone timeout.

scenarios.scenario: We need Claude connected to an internal HTTP tool service that authenticates with short-lived tokens minted by our single-sign-on helper command. Tokens expire mid-session, and the service exposes no OAuth endpoints of its own.

key.primary: MCP server configured with headersHelper: a command that writes a JSON object of headers to stdout, run fresh at each connection and automatically re-run with one retry when a call returns 401 or 403
key.rejected_alternative: A static Authorization header in the server's .mcp.json entry using ${TOKEN} environment-variable expansion
key.rejection_reason: Environment expansion resolves once from the ambient environment, so an expired short-lived token leaves the connection failing until restart. The docs name headersHelper as the mechanism for authentication schemes other than OAuth, such as Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO, and Claude Code re-runs the helper, reconnects, and retries the call once on 401/403.
key.lifecycle: helper runs in a shell with a 10-second timeout at session start, on every reconnect, and on a 401/403 retry; there is no caching, so the script owns any token reuse
key.failure_mode: the helper executes arbitrary shell commands, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted; a helper that exceeds 10 seconds or prints non-JSON breaks the connection entirely
key.version_caveat: automatic helper re-run and single retry on 401/403 requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later

sheets.primary: An HTTP-transport MCP server entry that uses `headersHelper` pointing at the SSO helper command (script path or inline shell). Claude Code runs the command at connection time and merges the JSON object it writes to stdout into the connection headers, so each connection carries a freshly minted short-lived token even though the service exposes no OAuth endpoints.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A static `headers` block with `"Authorization": "Bearer ${TOKEN}"` relying on environment-variable expansion in `.mcp.json`. Rejected because the value is resolved once when the config loads and cannot be re-minted when the token expires part way through a session.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness executes the helper, merges its headers over any static ones, and on a 401 or 403 re-runs it, reconnects, and retries the call once. The helper script itself owns token minting and any caching, since Claude Code deliberately does none.
sheets.context_boundary: The helper runs in its own shell process with a ten-second timeout, from the session's working directory (or the plugin root for a plugin-provided server). Only the resulting headers cross into the MCP connection; no token value ever enters the model's context window.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs fresh on each connection, meaning session start and every reconnect, plus once more on the automatic 401/403 retry. It applies for as long as the server entry exists and the server is enabled; there is no scheduled refresh in between, so mid-session expiry is handled by the retry path rather than proactively.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on the connection but can thrash: if the helper exceeds ten seconds, emits non-JSON, or the freshly minted token is rejected on the retry too, the server is flagged as needing authentication and its tools vanish mid-session. With no caching, a slow SSO helper is re-invoked on every reconnect. `headersHelper` executes arbitrary shell, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted.
sheets.version_caveat: The automatic re-run-and-retry on 401/403 requires v2.1.193 or later. For a plugin-provided server, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` substitution inside `headersHelper` and the plugin-root working directory require v2.1.195 or later (earlier versions passed the placeholder through literally). As of v2.1.207 a plugin `headersHelper` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` because the field is shell-parsed; put the value in `headers` or have the script read it from its own config.

sheets.primary: An MCP server entry using `headersHelper`: an `http` server pointing at the internal service, with `headersHelper` set to the SSO helper command, which Claude Code runs and whose JSON output it merges into the connection headers. The docs name this case directly as the mechanism for an authentication scheme other than OAuth, such as Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO. The helper must write a JSON object of string key-value pairs to stdout, for example `{"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}`.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A static `headers` entry with `${TOKEN}` environment-variable expansion in `.mcp.json`. Environment expansion is resolved once at config load, so it cannot produce a fresh token when the old one expires mid-session, which is the whole requirement.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code executes the helper command, merges its output into the connection headers, and re-runs it on authentication failure. The model never sees or handles the token.
sheets.context_boundary: The helper runs as a shell subprocess with a 10-second timeout, from the session's working directory, entirely outside the context window; only MCP tool results cross into the main session context. The minted token stays in the connection headers and never enters the transcript. Claude Code sets `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_NAME`, `CLAUDE_CODE_MCP_SERVER_URL`, and (for plugin-provided servers) `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` in the helper's environment so one script can serve several servers.
sheets.lifecycle: The helper runs fresh on each connection, at session start and on every reconnect, with no caching, so your script is responsible for any token reuse. It also re-runs on demand: a tool call that returns 401 or 403 causes Claude Code to re-run the helper, reconnect with the fresh headers, and retry the call once. It stops applying when the server is removed or disabled.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed per call, with a narrow recovery window. Mid-session expiry is only covered by that single automatic retry; if the re-minted token is also rejected, Claude Code marks the server as needing authentication in `/mcp` and the tools go away for the rest of the session. The 10-second shell timeout is a real hazard when the SSO helper itself needs an interactive prompt or a slow network round trip, and because there is no caching a chatty session re-runs the helper on every reconnect. Dynamic headers silently override any static `headers` of the same name.
sheets.version_caveat: The automatic re-run of the helper plus retry on 401/403 requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later. For a plugin-provided server, resolving a relative `headersHelper` path against the plugin root requires v2.1.195 or later, and before v2.1.195 plugin `headersHelper` passed the `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` placeholder through as a literal string. A plugin-provided `headersHelper` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` values because the command is shell-parsed; before v2.1.207 it did substitute them. `headersHelper` executes arbitrary shell commands, so at project or local scope it only runs after the workspace trust dialog is accepted.

sheets.primary: An MCP server on the HTTP transport configured with `headersHelper` pointing at the SSO helper, which prints a JSON object of header key/value pairs on stdout (for example `{"Authorization": "Bearer ..."}`). This is the documented path for a server that authenticates with something other than OAuth, such as Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A static `headers.Authorization` populated by `${VAR}` expansion in .mcp.json: the value is fixed when the config loads, so a token that expires mid-session leaves the server failing until restart, and dynamic headers override same-named static headers anyway.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: Claude Code executes the helper command and merges its output into the connection headers. The token never enters the model's context, and the model cannot influence which credential is used.
sheets.context_boundary: The helper runs in a shell subprocess outside the conversation, with a 10-second timeout from the session's working directory (or the plugin root for a plugin-provided server). Only bounded tool results cross into the session; header values never appear in the transcript.
sheets.lifecycle: The helper runs fresh on every connection, at session start and on each reconnect, with no caching, so the script owns any token reuse. From v2.1.193 a 401 or 403 on a tool call re-runs the helper, reconnects with fresh headers and retries the call once. At project or local scope it only runs after you accept the workspace trust dialog.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. If the retry also fails, the server is merely flagged as needing authentication in `/mcp` and its tools are absent for the rest of the session, which is indistinguishable to the model from a tool that declined. A helper that exceeds the 10-second timeout or emits non-JSON yields no headers and the connection is simply not authenticated.
sheets.version_caveat: The automatic re-run-and-retry on 401/403 requires v2.1.193+. A plugin-provided helper resolves relative paths against the plugin root only from v2.1.195+, and since v2.1.207 a plugin-provided `headersHelper` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` values (the server is reported as misconfigured); put those in the `headers` field instead.

sheets.primary: A local stdio MCP server acting as an authenticating proxy: it shells out to the SSO helper to mint a token just before each upstream call, caches it until shortly before expiry, and forwards the HTTP request to the internal service.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Registering the service directly as an http-transport MCP server with a static Authorization header taken from an environment variable.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness plus the proxy you write. Claude Code launches the proxy and speaks MCP to it; token freshness is entirely the proxy's job and never something the model is asked to manage.
sheets.context_boundary: The proxy is a separate local process, so the token lives in its memory and never enters the transcript. Only tool schemas and sanitized results cross into the session context.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the session connects the MCP server and lives as long as the session; refresh happens per request or on expiry, invisible to the conversation. It stops when the server is removed or the session ends.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed: if the SSO helper is not signed in or errors, tool calls fail rather than silently proceeding, which is the right shape but shows up as confusing mid-session breakage. The real hazard is leaking a token into the transcript through an unsanitized upstream error body.
sheets.version_caveat: Environment variable interpolation in .mcp.json and any --header value is resolved when the server is configured or launched, so it cannot express a mid-session refresh. I am not aware of a documented pre-request auth or token-refresh hook for HTTP MCP transports in Claude Code.

scenarios.scenario: Whenever our shared toolkit is active in a session, Claude should hear about new lines appended to the application's error log as they appear, for the whole session, without anyone asking it to start watching.

key.primary: A plugin background monitor: an entry in monitors/monitors.json running tail -F, whose stdout lines Claude Code delivers to Claude as notifications for the lifetime of the session
key.rejected_alternative: A SessionStart hook whose command launches tail -F as a detached background process
key.rejection_reason: A hook command runs to completion per event and has no channel for delivering output that arrives later into the conversation, so the detached tail's lines never reach Claude. Monitors are the documented component that Claude Code starts automatically when the plugin is active, keeps running all session, and whose every stdout line is delivered to Claude as a notification, with the name field preventing duplicate processes on reload.
key.lifecycle: starts at session start and on plugin reload with when set to always, or on first dispatch of a named skill with on-skill-invoke:<skill-name>; runs for the session lifetime
key.failure_mode: monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions, run unsandboxed at hook trust level, do not load for project-scope skills-directory plugins, and keep running after the plugin is disabled mid-session until the session ends
key.version_caveat: experimental component: declared under experimental.monitors in plugin.json, and the schema may change between releases while it stabilizes

sheets.primary: Hooks shipped in the plugin: a SessionStart hook that spawns a detached tailer writing new log lines to a spool file, plus a per-turn hook (UserPromptSubmit, or PostToolUse) that drains the spool and injects the new lines as additional context, with a SessionEnd hook to kill the tailer.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that tells Claude to launch tail -f as a background Bash task and poll its output.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness. Hooks fire on their events whatever the model intends, which is exactly what satisfies the requirement that nobody has to ask it to start watching.
sheets.context_boundary: The tailer runs completely outside the model. What crosses is only the drained lines the hook prints, injected into the main session context at turn boundaries, so it is near real time rather than a true push.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts at session start whenever the plugin is active and ends at session end, provided the cleanup hook actually kills the watcher; otherwise orphaned tailers accumulate across sessions.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and dangerously: if the hook or the tailer dies, Claude never hears about errors and has no signal that it has gone blind. The second practical failure is flooding, since a noisy log can eat the context window turn after turn, so the drain needs a hard line and byte cap.
sheets.version_caveat: Hook event names and the additional-context injection mechanism have changed across releases, and I am not certain which events currently accept injected context, so verify SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and SessionEnd behavior against the installed version. I also do not know whether MCP server-initiated notifications are surfaced to the model, which would be the cleaner push path if they are.

sheets.primary: A background monitor declared by the toolkit plugin in `monitors/monitors.json`, for example `{"name": "error-log", "command": "tail -F ./logs/error.log", "description": "Application error log", "when": "always"}`. Claude Code starts it automatically when the plugin is active and delivers every stdout line to Claude as a notification, which is exactly the documented no-one-has-to-ask-for-it case.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A SessionStart hook that launches a background tail: hooks return a single payload at the event, so SessionStart context attaches to the first turn only and there is no channel for a continuous stream of new lines for the rest of the session.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns starting the process and delivering each line as a notification; the model owns only whether it reacts to what it hears. Monitor commands run under the same permission rules as Bash.
sheets.context_boundary: The watched process runs outside the context window, but each stdout line is injected into the running main session as a notification, so a chatty log spends session context continuously for the whole session.
sheets.lifecycle: With `when: "always"` (the default) it starts at session start and on plugin reload; `on-skill-invoke:<skill>` defers it to the first dispatch of that skill. It runs for the lifetime of the session, and disabling the plugin mid-session does not stop an already-running monitor: it stops when the session ends. After a plugin update, monitors need a session restart, not `/reload-plugins`.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and silently. Monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions and are skipped wherever the Monitor tool is unavailable, namely Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry, or when `DISABLE_TELEMETRY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` is set. They also do not load at all for a project-scope skills-directory plugin, and they run unsandboxed at the same trust level as hooks.
sheets.version_caveat: Monitors are an experimental plugin component: declare them under `experimental.monitors` in plugin.json, since the top-level key still works but `claude plugin validate` warns and a future release will require `experimental.*`, and the schema may change between releases. A monitor command cannot reference `${user_config.*}` and is rejected with an error; before v2.1.207 those values were substituted.

sheets.primary: A plugin background monitor: add `monitors/monitors.json` at the plugin root with an entry whose `command` is `tail -F ./logs/error.log`, a `name`, a `description`, and `when` left at its default `"always"`. Claude Code starts each monitor automatically when the plugin is active, and every stdout line from the command is delivered to Claude as a notification during the session, which is precisely 'without anyone asking it to start watching'. This is the docs' own worked example.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A SessionStart hook that launches `tail -F` as a background Bash process. The hook can start the process, but hook output is injected once at the hook's moment; it has no channel for pushing each subsequent line into the conversation as it appears, so it gives startup automation without the ongoing delivery.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code spawns the monitor process when the plugin is active and delivers each stdout line as a notification; the model does not decide to start or poll it, it only reacts to what arrives.
sheets.context_boundary: The `tail` process runs as a persistent background process in the session working directory, outside the context window. Each stdout line crosses the boundary into the main session context as a notification, and the `description` is what shows in the task panel and notification summaries. Because every line crosses, the log's volume is directly a context cost.
sheets.lifecycle: With `when` at `"always"` the monitor starts at session start and on plugin reload; `"on-skill-invoke:<skill-name>"` would instead start it the first time that skill is dispatched. It runs for the lifetime of the session. Notably, if you disable the plugin mid-session Claude Code does not stop monitors that are already running; they stop when the session ends. After a plugin update, monitors keep using the previous version's path and require a session restart rather than `/reload-plugins`.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and is silently skipped where unsupported, then floods where supported. Monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions, run unsandboxed at the same trust level as hooks, and are skipped on hosts where the Monitor tool is unavailable, so a CI or headless run just never watches anything and nobody is told. Where it does run, a noisy error log pushes an unbounded stream of notifications into the context window and can crowd out the actual task. The `name` field is what prevents duplicate processes when the plugin reloads, so a careless rename spawns a second tail.
sheets.version_caveat: Monitors are an experimental plugin component: the manifest schema may change between releases, and declaring them at the top level of `plugin.json` still works but `claude plugin validate` warns and a future release will require `experimental.monitors`. Monitor commands cannot reference `${user_config.*}` values and are rejected with an error if they do; before v2.1.207 those values were substituted. The underlying Monitor tool is not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry, nor when `DISABLE_TELEMETRY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` is set.

Claude Code starts it automatically whenever the plugin is active and delivers each stdout line to Claude as a session notification.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill instructing Claude to launch `tail -F` as a background Bash task. Rejected because it only runs once someone invokes the skill and depends on the model remembering to start and re-check it, which is exactly the 'without anyone asking' requirement it fails.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness: Claude Code spawns and supervises the process for the lifetime of the session and pushes every emitted line in as a notification. The model owns only how it reacts to those lines.
sheets.context_boundary: The `tail` process runs outside the model's context, in the session working directory. Every stdout line crosses into the main session context as a notification, so a chatty log spends context window directly and continuously.
sheets.lifecycle: With the default `when: "always"` it starts at session start and on plugin reload; `"on-skill-invoke:<skill-name>"` instead defers it to the first dispatch of that skill. It runs for the rest of the session, and disabling the plugin mid-session does not stop an already-running monitor: it stops when the session ends. Picking up a new plugin version's monitor requires a session restart, not `/reload-plugins`.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions and are skipped entirely on hosts where the Monitor tool is unavailable, so headless or hosted runs silently get nothing. A high-volume error log floods the context window, and a monitor whose command dies (missing file, a relative path resolved against the wrong working directory) produces silence that reads exactly like 'no errors'. They run unsandboxed at hook trust level.
