scenarios.scenario: Security approved a third-party hosted integration for read-only use, but the vendor's sign-in service advertises write and admin permissions as well. We must guarantee that the credential stored on engineers' machines can never authorize a write, not merely that the assistant declines to perform one.

key.primary: Pin oauth.scopes in the server's .mcp.json entry (a space-separated string per RFC 6749) so Claude Code requests only the approved scope subset during the authorization flow and the issued token carries nothing more
key.rejected_alternative: Permission deny rules or a PreToolUse hook blocking the integration's write tools by name
key.rejection_reason: Deny rules and hooks constrain which tools the client calls, but the token in storage would still carry write scopes if granted, so any leak or bypass is a write credential. The docs call oauth.scopes the supported way to restrict an MCP server to a security-team-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more scopes than you want to grant; the authorization server then issues a token limited to those scopes, with offline_access appended when advertised so refresh keeps working.
key.lifecycle: applies during the OAuth authorization flow; takes precedence over authServerMetadataUrl and discovered metadata; re-authentication after a 403 insufficient_scope reuses the same pinned set
key.failure_mode: a tool that legitimately needs a scope outside the pinned set fails with 403 insufficient_scope until you widen oauth.scopes and re-authenticate, and the pin silently overrides scopes supplied by a configured metadata URL
key.version_caveat: none for the pin itself; the related default of not requesting the full scopes_supported catalog changed in v2.1.196

sheets.primary: The MCP server entry with `oauth.scopes` pinned to the read-only scope string, which the docs name as the supported way to restrict a server to a security-team-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more scopes than you want to grant. Distribute that entry where engineers cannot widen it, meaning managed settings rather than a hand-editable local file.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Permission rules or a PreToolUse hook denying the server's write tools: that stops the assistant from calling them, but the credential sitting on the machine still carries write and admin authority, which is precisely what the requirement rules out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Shared, and the boundary matters: Claude Code (harness) pins which scopes are requested in the authorization flow, but the vendor's authorization server is what actually mints a token limited to them. The model is out of the loop entirely and cannot request more.
sheets.context_boundary: The browser authorization flow and the resulting token live outside the conversation, in Claude Code's credential storage. Only tool results cross into the session; the model never sees the token or its scopes.
sheets.lifecycle: The pin applies when the engineer runs the sign-in flow, and takes precedence over both `authServerMetadataUrl` and the scopes discovered at `/.well-known`. `offline_access` is appended when advertised so the token refreshes without a new browser sign-in, and a later re-authentication uses the same pinned scopes. It stops applying if the entry is edited or the credential is cleared.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed at the call: a write tool returns 403 `insufficient_scope`, and Claude Code re-authenticates with the same pinned scopes rather than widening them, so the write never succeeds. The residual risk is configuration, not runtime: leaving `oauth.scopes` unset silently reverts to server-determined scopes, and a user-writable .mcp.json can be widened by the user.
sheets.version_caveat: `oauth.scopes` applies to the OAuth transports (HTTP, and SSE which is deprecated); WebSocket authentication is header-only and stdio is unaffected. From v2.1.196, when `oauth.scopes` is unset Claude Code requests only the scope from `WWW-Authenticate` or protected-resource metadata and no longer requests the full `scopes_supported` catalog.

sheets.primary: An MCP server entry with `oauth.scopes` pinned to the read-only subset, for example `"oauth": { "scopes": "issues:read search:read" }` on the `http` server. The docs call this the supported way to restrict an MCP server to a security-team-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more scopes than you want to grant. Because it pins the scopes requested during the authorization flow, the access token the vendor mints physically lacks write and admin, which is the credential-level guarantee asked for. Push it through managed settings so engineers cannot widen it locally.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook or a `deny` permission rule blocking the write-shaped MCP tools. That constrains what the assistant is allowed to call, not what the credential can authorize; the token on disk would still carry write scope and any other process, or a bypassed permission mode, could use it. The requirement explicitly rules out 'the assistant declines'.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Ultimately the vendor's authorization server, with the harness owning the request. Claude Code sends the pinned `scope` parameter in the authorization request and stores whatever token comes back; the vendor decides what that token may do. The model is out of the loop entirely, which is the point.
sheets.context_boundary: The authorization handshake happens out of context in the browser and the resulting token lives in Claude Code's credential storage, never in the transcript. Only the read-only tool definitions and their results cross into the main session context window.
sheets.lifecycle: The pinned scopes apply at every authorization flow for that server, from the first sign-in onward, and `oauth.scopes` takes precedence over both `authServerMetadataUrl` and the scopes discovered at `/.well-known`. If the server later returns 403 `insufficient_scope` for a tool call, Claude Code re-authenticates with the same pinned scopes rather than escalating. It stops applying if the field is removed, at which point the MCP server determines the requested scope set again.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed against the credential, which is the desired behaviour: a write tool call comes back 403 `insufficient_scope` and re-authentication does not widen the grant. The residual risk is not technical but configurational: `oauth.scopes` is a config field, so at user or project scope an engineer can edit it and re-authenticate with broader scopes, and the guarantee only holds if it is deployed through managed settings. Note also that Claude Code appends `offline_access` to the pinned scopes when the authorization server advertises it in `scopes_supported`, so the effective grant is not byte-identical to what you wrote.
sheets.version_caveat: The default behaviour when `oauth.scopes` is unset changed in v2.1.196: Claude Code now requests the scope from the server's `WWW-Authenticate` header or its protected resource metadata and sends no `scope` parameter when neither provides one, rather than requesting the full `scopes_supported` catalog. On earlier versions, leaving scopes unpinned against a provider that advertises admin scopes could request that whole catalog and be rejected with `invalid_scope`. Metadata fetched from a configured `authServerMetadataUrl` still supplies its `scopes_supported` as the requested scopes.

sheets.primary: The guarantee has to live in the credential, so the control belongs at the vendor: authorize through an app registration or account role that can only ever be granted read scopes, so the token minted by the browser sign-in is physically incapable of a write. Claude Code then connects to it as an ordinary remote MCP server.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Permission deny rules in settings targeting the write-shaped MCP tool names.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Neither the model nor the harness: the vendor's authorization server owns it. Anything Claude Code enforces only governs Claude's use of a token that would still be write-capable in anyone else's hands, which is exactly the weaker property the requirement rules out.
sheets.context_boundary: Not a context question. Scope enforcement happens server side at the vendor, and the session only ever sees tool results or authorization errors.
sheets.lifecycle: Fixed at authorization time and persists for the life of the grant. It stops applying the moment someone re-authorizes through the broader consent screen, so the read-only role must be the only path engineers can take.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed at the vendor, which is the property asked for: a write attempt returns an authorization error instead of being argued out of. The realistic failure is procedural, an engineer re-running sign-in and accepting the full scope list, and no local Claude Code setting will detect that.
sheets.version_caveat: I am not aware of any documented way to constrain requested OAuth scopes from claude mcp add. Note that its --scope flag selects the configuration location (local, project or user), not OAuth scopes, and confusing the two is an easy way to believe you have limited a credential when you have not.

sheets.primary: Pin the OAuth scopes in the server's MCP configuration: an `"oauth": { "scopes": "<read-only scopes>" }` object on the HTTP server entry in `.mcp.json`. This is the documented mechanism for restricting a server to a security-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more, and it constrains the token actually minted on each engineer's machine rather than constraining the assistant.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Permission deny rules (or a PreToolUse hook) blocking the server's write and admin tools by name. Rejected because that only stops the assistant from calling them: the credential sitting on the machine would still carry write authority, which is the exact distinction security asked for.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Shared between the harness and the vendor's authorization server. Claude Code sends only the pinned `scope` parameter during authorization; the identity provider is what actually limits the issued token. The model has no role, which is the point.
sheets.context_boundary: Scope configuration lives in the MCP config and the resulting token in secure storage (system keychain on macOS, credentials file otherwise). Neither crosses into the model's context window; only tool results do.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies at the authorization flow: first sign-in and every re-authentication, including the automatic re-auth after a 403. `oauth.scopes` takes precedence over both `authServerMetadataUrl` and the scopes discovered at `/.well-known`. A token minted before the pin was added keeps its original grant, so existing engineers must `claude mcp logout` and sign in again for the restriction to take effect.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed at the API boundary: a tool needing a scope outside the pinned set returns 403 `insufficient_scope`, and Claude Code re-authenticates with the same pinned scopes instead of widening, so the write path stays dead until someone deliberately edits the config. The residual risk is upstream: the guarantee is only as strong as the provider's scope model, so a service that issues coarse-grained tokens or ignores the requested scope can still hand back an over-privileged credential. Verify against the token the provider actually issues.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires the HTTP transport, since OAuth does not apply to stdio and WebSocket is header-auth only. As of v2.1.196 Claude Code stops requesting the full `scopes_supported` catalog when `oauth.scopes` is unset (that behavior was triggering `invalid_scope` rejections from providers advertising admin-only scopes), and it appends `offline_access` to the pinned set when the authorization server advertises it, so the pinned list is not literally the only scope requested. Metadata fetched from a configured `authServerMetadataUrl` still supplies `scopes_supported` when `oauth.scopes` is left unset.

scenarios.scenario: Everyone working in one repository needs the same connection to our staging-database tool service, picked up automatically from a fresh clone, with each person consenting once before it first runs. No other repository will ever use this connection.

key.primary: A project-scoped MCP server: a .mcp.json file at the repository root, committed to version control, with Claude Code's built-in per-user approval prompt (resettable via claude mcp reset-project-choices)
key.rejected_alternative: Package the server configuration as a plugin and stand up an internal marketplace to distribute it
key.rejection_reason: For a single project the docs designate the checked-in .mcp.json project scope as the team-sharing path, complete with a per-user security approval flow before first use. A plugin plus marketplace adds hosting, install and enablement steps, and version machinery whose documented payoffs, reuse across multiple projects and versioned releases, this need explicitly lacks.
key.lifecycle: loaded from .mcp.json at the project root; each user approves it before first use; sits below local scope and above user scope in the name-matching precedence order
key.failure_mode: the server sits at Pending approval for each user until they approve interactively, and the config lives in exactly one repo: the day a second repository needs the same server, the entry gets copy-pasted and drifts, which is the point where a plugin becomes the right call
key.version_caveat: as of v2.1.196, enableAllProjectMcpServers or enabledMcpjsonServers committed in project settings cannot self-approve servers in a workspace the user has not trusted

sheets.primary: A .mcp.json at the repository root, committed to version control, declaring the staging-database MCP server. Project-scoped MCP configuration is picked up from a fresh clone, and Claude Code asks each user to approve the project's servers once before they are allowed to run.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Adding the same server at user scope (claude mcp add --scope user), which would follow each engineer into every other repository.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness: it reads the file, gates on the per-user approval prompt, and records the decision. The model cannot enable a server the user has not approved.
sheets.context_boundary: The server is its own process or a remote endpoint; once approved, its tool schemas sit in the main session context on every turn, and results cross per call.
sheets.lifecycle: The first session in the clone triggers the consent prompt, the approval is stored per user per project and persists after that, and a changed server definition can re-prompt. It applies only while working inside that repository.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed: a declined or not-yet-approved server is simply absent, and Claude often cannot explain why the tool is missing. The other real risk is credential leakage, since anything hardcoded in a committed .mcp.json is shared with the whole team, so use ${ENV_VAR} interpolation instead.
sheets.version_caveat: Environment variable interpolation in .mcp.json and the enabledMcpjsonServers / enableAllProjectMcpServers settings arrived in later releases and I do not know their exact minimum versions. A blanket allow-all setting, whether local or pushed by managed policy, would defeat the once-per-person consent requirement.

sheets.primary: A project-scoped MCP server: a `.mcp.json` at the repository root, committed to version control, added with `claude mcp add --transport http <name> --scope project <url>`. It loads only in that project, arrives with a fresh clone, and Claude Code prompts each person for approval before it is ever used.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Bundling the same server inside a team plugin. Rejected because plugin servers install per user across scopes and are a distribution channel aimed at many repositories, whereas project `.mcp.json` is the repository-bound mechanism that already carries the one-time per-user consent prompt.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness: Claude Code reads `.mcp.json`, holds the entry at pending approval until the user accepts, records the decision per user, and starts the connection. Nothing depends on the model.
sheets.context_boundary: Scoped to sessions opened in that project directory. The server runs out of process and only tool results cross into the session window. Keep the credential out of the committed file by using `${VAR}` or `${VAR:-default}` expansion, which works in `command`, `args`, `env`, `url`, and `headers`.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated at session start in that project. Approval is a one-time per-user decision that persists until reset with `claude mcp reset-project-choices`. It never loads in another project, and a local- or user-scoped server with the same name takes precedence over it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed: until approved the server shows as pending approval and its tools do not exist, which can read to Claude as if the capability were never configured. A cloned repository cannot self-approve, so `enableAllProjectMcpServers` or `enabledMcpjsonServers` committed to `.claude/settings.json` is ignored until the workspace trust dialog is accepted. A missing environment variable does not block loading either: Claude Code warns and passes the literal `${VAR}` through, producing a confusing downstream auth failure.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.196 `claude mcp list`/`get` read `.mcp.json` approvals from checked-in settings only after the workspace is trusted; before v2.1.207 an untracked `.claude/settings.local.json` could approve servers in a never-trusted folder. A JSON entry with a `url` must declare `"type"` explicitly or the server is skipped (the error message was clearer from v2.1.202). A `disabledMcpjsonServers` entry in any settings file rejects the server outright.

sheets.primary: A project-scoped MCP server: add it with `claude mcp add --transport http staging-db --scope project <url>`, which writes `.mcp.json` at the project root, and check that file into version control so everyone on the team gets the same MCP tools and services. Project scope is the only one of the three that is shared via version control and is limited to the current project, which matches 'from a fresh clone' and 'no other repository' exactly.
sheets.rejected_alternative: User scope (`--scope user`, stored in `~/.claude.json`). It is private to each machine so it would not arrive with a clone, and it is available across all your projects, which directly violates the 'no other repository will ever use this connection' constraint.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, gated on a per-user consent prompt. Claude Code discovers `.mcp.json` in the project root, holds the server until the user approves it, and then owns the connection. The model has no say in whether the server loads.
sheets.context_boundary: Config crosses into the repository through git; the server's tool definitions and results cross into each engineer's main session context window once approved. Credentials do not travel in `.mcp.json` if you use OAuth or `headersHelper`, which is why you should not embed a token there even though the file is shared.
sheets.lifecycle: The server is discovered when a session opens in that project directory and connects once the user approves it; the approval is recorded per user so the prompt appears only on first use. `claude mcp reset-project-choices` clears those recorded approvals so the prompt returns. Scope precedence is local, then project, then user, so a same-named local entry silently wins over the shared one, with the entire entry taken from the winning source and no field merging.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed, which is safe but surprising in automation: for security reasons Claude Code prompts for approval before using project-scoped servers from `.mcp.json`, and until someone approves, `claude mcp list` and `claude mcp get <name>` show the server as 'Pending approval (run `claude` to approve)' with none of its tools present. A rejected server shows as 'Rejected (see disabledMcpjsonServers in settings)'. A non-interactive or CI session cannot answer the prompt, so it needs `enabledMcpjsonServers` in settings instead. The quiet failure is a teammate who declined once and then reports the tools 'missing' rather than 'not approved'.
sheets.version_caveat: The scope names were renamed: older versions called today's `local` scope `project`, and today's `user` scope `global`, so older team documentation and scripts using `--scope project` may mean the private per-machine scope. Environment-variable expansion inside a project-scoped `.mcp.json` needs a default for session variables, for example `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}`, because that variable is set in the server's environment rather than Claude Code's own; plugin-provided configs substitute it directly and need no default.

sheets.primary: A project-scoped MCP server checked into the repository's `.mcp.json` at the project root, added with `claude mcp add --transport http staging-db --scope project <url>`. Project scope is the documented team-collaboration scope: the file is version controlled, so a fresh clone carries the connection and nothing else has to be set up per person.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A user-scoped server in `~/.claude.json`: it would load in every project on the machine, which the requirement explicitly excludes, and each teammate would have to add it by hand rather than getting it from the clone.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: for security reasons Claude Code prompts each user for approval before using a project-scoped server from `.mcp.json`, and records that person's choice. The model has no say in whether the server connects.
sheets.context_boundary: Sessions started in that repository only. The server definition crosses via git rather than the conversation; its tool names load into the session window and results come back bounded by the MCP output cap.
sheets.lifecycle: On the first interactive run in a fresh clone the server sits at `Pending approval` until the person approves it once; the choice then persists for that user. Reset it with `claude mcp reset-project-choices`, and note that a local-scope entry of the same name takes precedence over the project one.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails absent rather than erroring: until it is approved the server is not connected, so a headless `claude -p` run in a fresh clone silently has no staging-db tools. A cloned repository cannot approve its own servers, so committed `enableAllProjectMcpServers` or `enabledMcpjsonServers` in `.claude/settings.json` are ignored in an untrusted folder, and a `disabledMcpjsonServers` entry in any settings file rejects the server outright.
sheets.version_caveat: As of v2.1.196 `claude mcp list`/`get` read `.mcp.json` approvals from non-checked-in settings only after you trust the workspace by running `claude` in it and accepting the trust dialog. Before v2.1.207 an untracked `.claude/settings.local.json` could approve servers in a folder that had never been trusted.

scenarios.scenario: Our distributed toolkit needs npm dependencies installed on each user's machine at first run, and those installed modules must keep working after the toolkit updates instead of being stranded or wiped when a new version lands.

key.primary: Install into ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}, the persistent per-plugin data directory under ~/.claude/plugins/data/, via a SessionStart hook that diffs the bundled package.json against a stored copy and reinstalls when they differ
key.rejected_alternative: Run npm install into ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} on first run and point the bundled server at that node_modules
key.rejection_reason: The plugin root is the versioned cache directory: its path changes on every update and the previous version's directory is removed about two weeks later, so the docs say to treat it as ephemeral and not write state there. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA} is documented for exactly this: installed dependencies such as node_modules or Python virtual environments that survive plugin updates and are deleted only on uninstall from the last scope (unless --keep-data).
key.lifecycle: the data directory is created on first reference, survives every plugin update, and is deleted when the plugin is uninstalled from its last scope; the install hook fires at SessionStart
key.failure_mode: because the directory outlives versions, a bare existence check misses updates that change the dependency manifest; skipping the documented manifest-diff pattern leaves users running new plugin code against stale dependencies

sheets.primary: A plugin whose first-run installer is a SessionStart hook: it checks a marker or lockfile and, when missing or when the recorded dependency version differs, installs the npm dependencies into a stable per-plugin data directory outside the plugin install path (for example under the user's ~/.claude data area keyed by plugin name), so the module tree survives a plugin content swap.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Running npm install into ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/node_modules on first use.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Harness fires the hook on schedule; your installer script owns idempotence, the version marker, and deciding whether to reuse or rebuild the existing module tree.
sheets.context_boundary: It runs entirely outside the model's context as a hook subprocess. Only a short success or failure line should ever cross into the session, never the npm output.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs at every session start but does real work only when the marker is absent or the pinned dependency set changed, exiting immediately otherwise. Disabling the plugin stops the hook but does not clean the data directory, which is the deliberate tradeoff for surviving updates.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open in the worst way: a failed install at session start is easy to miss and every later command dies with a confusing module-not-found rather than the real cause, so the hook must emit a loud explicit error. Also expect a slow first session, races when two sessions start at once, and breakage on offline or proxied machines.
sheets.version_caveat: I am not aware of a documented plugin post-install lifecycle hook, which is why this is anchored to SessionStart; check whether the current release adds one. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} is documented for referencing plugin files but points at content that can be replaced wholesale on update, which is the whole reason dependencies must not live under it.

sheets.primary: A `SessionStart` command hook in the plugin's `hooks/hooks.json` that installs the npm dependencies into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, the persistent directory that survives plugin updates. Use the documented pattern: diff the bundled `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json` against the copy in the data directory and run `npm install` only when they differ, then point runtime consumers at `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/node_modules` via `NODE_PATH`.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Installing into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` at first run: that path changes on every plugin update and the previous version's directory is cleaned up roughly two weeks later, so the modules are stranded or wiped exactly as the requirement warns.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns firing the hook on every session start; the install script owns correctness. The manifest-diff logic, not Claude Code, is what decides whether a reinstall is needed.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs in a subprocess outside the conversation, and the installed modules live in the user-level data directory `~/.claude/plugins/data/{id}/`, not in session context. Nothing but an error notice would reach the model.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires at every SessionStart and is a no-op when the stored manifest matches the bundled one; it reinstalls on first run and again whenever an update changes package.json. The data directory outlives every plugin version and is deleted only when the plugin is uninstalled from its last scope, unless you pass `--keep-data`.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open: SessionStart cannot block, so a failed `npm install` leaves the session running with missing modules and only a stderr notice. The documented command deliberately removes the copied manifest on failure so the next session retries, and a bare directory-exists check would be the classic wrong version of this, since the data directory outlives any single plugin version.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate, experimental flag, or plan restriction is documented for `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` or for SessionStart hooks in the plugins reference. The behaviour to plan around instead is that a mid-session plugin update keeps hooks and MCP/LSP servers on the previous path until `/reload-plugins`, and monitors until a session restart.

sheets.primary: A `SessionStart` hook in the plugin's `hooks/hooks.json` that installs into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, the per-plugin persistent directory at `~/.claude/plugins/data/{id}/` that survives plugin updates and is created on first reference. Use the documented pattern: `diff` the bundled `package.json` against the copy in the data directory, and on any difference copy it over and run `npm install` there; bundled scripts then resolve modules through it, for example an MCP server entry with `"NODE_PATH": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/node_modules"`.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Installing `node_modules` into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` alongside the shipped code. Rejected because the plugin root path changes on every update and the superseded version directory is pruned about fourteen days later, so the installed modules are stranded and then wiped.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness fires the SessionStart hook, creates and resolves `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, and substitutes the placeholder in hook commands and in MCP `command`/`args`/`env`. The install script owns whether the dependency state is actually correct.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook runs as a shell process at session start, outside the model's context; only hook output and failures cross back. The data directory is keyed to the plugin identifier and is shared across every project and session on that machine, unlike the per-version plugin root.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires on every session start, but the manifest diff makes it a no-op after the first successful install and re-installs only when an update ships a changed `package.json`. It stops applying when the plugin is uninstalled from its last scope, at which point the data directory is deleted by default (the `/plugin` interface shows its size and prompts; `--keep-data` preserves it).
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and adds startup latency: if `npm install` fails, nothing blocks the session and the breakage surfaces later as module-not-found from a bundled script, which is why the documented pattern deletes the copied manifest on failure so the next session retries. The classic bug is checking only whether the directory exists, which never detects a dependency manifest changed by an update. A mid-session plugin update also keeps hook commands and MCP servers on the previous version's path until `/reload-plugins`.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires a Claude Code version that supports `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, which resolves in hook and monitor commands and in MCP `command`, `args`, and `env` (and LSP `command`, `args`, `env`, `workspaceFolder`). As of v2.1.207 a hook command cannot reference `${user_config.*}` because the field is shell-parsed, so a configurable registry or token must come from the environment or a config file the script reads. Uninstall deletes the data directory unless `--keep-data` is passed.

sheets.primary: A plugin `SessionStart` hook that installs into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, the persistent directory that survives plugin updates and is documented for exactly this use: installed dependencies such as `node_modules` or Python virtual environments, generated code, and caches. Use the docs' recommended pattern rather than a bare existence check: `diff -q "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json" "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/package.json" || (cd "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}" && cp "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json" . && npm install) || rm -f "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/package.json"`, then point consumers at it with `NODE_PATH=${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/node_modules`.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Running `npm install` into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` from the same hook. That is the trap this scenario describes: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` changes when the plugin updates, so every update strands the installed modules in the old version directory, which is itself cleaned up automatically about two weeks later.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness runs the hook and resolves `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` (to `~/.claude/plugins/data/{id}/`, created on first reference), and the hook script owns the install decision. The model is not involved and is not asked to run `npm install`.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook executes as a subprocess at session start, outside the context window; only whatever it writes to stdout crosses into the session context, so the install should stay quiet. The installed `node_modules` are then read by MCP or LSP subprocesses through `NODE_PATH`, also outside the context window. `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, and `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` are all exported as environment variables to hook processes and to MCP and LSP server subprocesses.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs on `SessionStart`, every session, but does real work only on first run and after an update whose `package.json` differs from the stored copy, because `diff` exits nonzero when the stored copy is missing or differs. The data directory outlives any single plugin version and is deleted automatically when you uninstall the plugin from the last scope where it is installed.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open at install time and then breaks downstream: the session continues even if `npm install` fails, and the component that needed the modules errors later at first use, far from the cause. The pattern's trailing `rm` removes the copied manifest so the next session retries, which is a deliberate self-heal rather than a silent poison. The specific mistake the docs warn about is checking only for the directory's existence: because the data directory outlives any single plugin version, an existence check cannot detect when an update changes the plugin's dependency manifest, so users keep running against stale dependencies.
sheets.version_caveat: Persistence is not unconditional: the data directory is deleted automatically on uninstall from the last scope, the `/plugin` interface shows its size and prompts first, and the CLI deletes by default unless you pass `--keep-data`. Related timing gates: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` changes on update and the previous version's directory is removed about 14 days later, and when a plugin updates mid-session hooks, MCP servers and LSP servers keep the old path until `/reload-plugins`, while monitors require a full session restart.
